paper_title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Forming an accurate theory-of-mind (ToM) is key to successful multi-agent collaboration and requires reasoning under uncertainty to capture multiple possible partner states. This is hard to do in the text representation space native to large language model (LLM) agents, which more easily describe a single partner state. To address this challenge, we introduce ToM2Vec, which learns to form abstract theories-of-mind in a rich latent space via a fixed budget of continuous reasoning tokens. During training, supervision for these tokens comes from the partner's actual thoughts, which the ToM tokens are trained to abstract and match. At test-time, ToM tokens are generated by each agent and act as conditioners for that agent's thoughts and actions. Across several environments covering collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive settings (Overcooked-AI, multiparty negotiation, Decrypto, Hanabi, and Collab Escape/Capture), we evaluate ToM2Vec's ability to support multi-agent interactions and collaboration, finding consistent improvements over the base model and a variety of competitive trained and prompted baselines. We show that latent reasoning is critical, with performance dropping when reasoning is expressed in text. Moreover, we show that ToM2Vec training generalizes to partner model families not seen at train-time, including a proprietary model (GPT-5.4). In our analysis, we provide evidence that the latent tokens encode a ToM, rather than task-specific information: ToM2Vec's tokens improve the agent's ability to directly answer questions about partner beliefs, desires, and next actions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Humans have the ability to coordinate with each other remarkably well, often with little or no explicit communication. For instance, chefs can prepare meal together, teammates can execute play, 1Code: https://github.com/nsivaku/tom2vec 1 and negotiators can converge on deal, each anticipating what the other will do and acting accordingly. This capacity for joint action rests on each agents Theory of Mind (ToM): the ability to model another agents unobserved mental state based on observed behaviors (Premack and Woodruff, 1978). Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that must act alongside partner agents (human or AI) in both collaborative and competitive tasks (Duan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Stengel-Eskin et al., 2024; Kosinski, 2024; Xu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2026). To succeed in these settings, an agent needs strong working ToM (Bakhtin et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025a). This ToM allows the agent to infer partners goals, beliefs, and likely next actions, enabling it to coordinate with less explicit communication and adapt to counterparts strategy on the fly (Baker et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2020). Making these kinds of inferences can be seen as form of world modeling directed at another agent (Raileanu et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2022; Chernyavskiy et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). As in world modeling, it is often important to form an abstract model that can superimpose multiple possibilities, in this case of the partners intent (Xie et al., 2021; Chernyavskiy et al., 2025). general sketch of the partners beliefs and intentions is often sufficient, and excessive fidelity can be inefficient and in fact harmful to the task (Mu et al., 2026); for example, when two chefs have to coordinate in crowded kitchen, one does not need to predict what the other wants for breakfast tomorrow (which might even be distraction), but does need to predict if the other needs shared resources. Given this goal of abstraction, key challenge for ToM agents lies in building an abstract representation that retains enough information about the partners potential future paths to support prediction and planning, while lifting unnecessary details. We argue that natural language is poor medium Figure 1: Left: Vanilla LLM agents (using Qwen3-8B) each reason only about their own plan. Both independently conclude they should fetch dish from the dispenser, producing redundant and conflicting behavior. Middle: Language ToM Agents are able to more frequently consider their partners next actions, but they often commit to single line of reasoning without considering other potential paths. Right: Our method TOM2VEC is used to train an agent (blue hat) with stronger ToM capabilities; that agent considers what the untrained partner agent (green hat) is doing before making its own decision. for this kind of abstraction, as expressing another agents intent or state linguistically tends to commit the agent to single estimate of the partner, even when many distinct hypotheses are possible. Instead, we argue that modeling another agent may be more akin to forming latent world model (LeCun, 2022), where abstractions are formed in the models latent space rather than its output space (see Figure 1). Latent reasoning paradigms offer precisely this kind of latent-space abstraction as natural alternative to verbalized reasoning, where latent thought tokens can superimpose several candidate chains-of-thought rather than fixing to one (Hao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b; Shi et al., 2026). Similarly, we argue that representation of partner should be able to superimpose multiple hypotheses about the partners goals and intentions, and that ToM agent should be able to predict these representations and consider alternatives before committing to decision. To this end, we introduce TOM2VEC to directly learn these latent representations of the partner agent. TOM2VEC trains the agent to predict, from its own point-of-view, fixed number of continuous latent embeddings that abstract over its partners thoughts; in other words, it teaches the main agent to perform mind-reading task about its partner. During training, we obtain supervision for these latent embeddings by abstracting training partners actual next thoughts into continuous latent tokens to serve as representation of its reasoning. We train the agents generated latent embeddings to match the partners hidden states under cosine similarity objective (see Figure 2); during training, we use the same model for both agent and partner, as their representation spaces must be shared. At test-time (where partner reasoning is not available) an agent trained with TOM2VEC then generates its own latent thought tokens, intended to capture ToM about the partner. Interestingly, we show that at test-time, our training generalizes to other partner models, including closed-source proprietary model that is stronger than the training partner. We evaluate TOM2VEC across cooperative and competitive tasks, including (1) Overcooked (Carroll et al., 2019), cooperative cooking environment, (2) multi-party LLM negotiation (Abdelnabi et al., 2024), (3) Decrypto (Lupu et al., 2025), ToM task where two agents attempt to pass secret messages without being decoded by an interceptor agent, (4) Hanabi (Agashe et al., 2025), cooperative card game with hidden information, and (5) Collab Escape/Capture (Agashe et al., 2025), two collaborative coordination tasks. Across these domains, TOM2VEC delivers consistent improvements over competitive baselines. Relative to the untrained model (Qwen3-8B), training with TOM2VEC improves the average Overcooked score by 12.0 points and raises negotiation deal success from 62.0% to 71.0%. It also outperforms approaches that prompt agents to consider their partners intentions or train them to explicitly 2 verbalize their partners reasoning, supporting the value of learning latent partner representations. In Overcooked, these benefits extend to unseen partners from different model families: TOM2VEC improves over the base agent by 17.3 points on average with GPT-5.4 partner and matches or exceeds the base agent with Gemma-4 partner, despite training only with Qwen3-8B partner. Our analysis further examines to what extent TOM2VEC learns representations that capture partners evolving beliefs. We directly test whether these representations better support inferences about partners beliefs, desires, and next actions (i.e., Baker et al. (2011)s Bayesian ToM modeling) within given environment state. We also test whether the latent tokens encode partner-specific reasoning by deliberately corrupting the context used to derive them. Latents derived from the partners actual context assign lower perplexity to its true reasoning than those derived from an altered layout or an adversarial intent, supporting the interpretation that they capture contextsensitive information about the partner rather than only generic signals useful for coordination. We complement this analysis with additional results in the appendix, showing that TOM2VEC helps in Sally-Anne-style false-belief tests, and that the representations learned by TOM2VEC support belief revision given new evidence.

sections.title: 2.2 Modeling Partners via Latent Reasoning
sections.content: Under partial observability, the main agent must anticipate its partners behavior without observing the partners complete history and reasoning. We train Bθ to predict fixed budget of continuous latent vectors from the main agents own context: ˆzt = (cid:0)ˆzt,1, . . . , ˆzt,K (cid:1) = LatentK(Bθ; cM ), Here, LatentK denotes autoregressive steps in the models hidden space. To perform these steps, we follow recent work on latent reasoning (Hao et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2025) and treat the last layers hidden state at each step as the next steps input embedding, rather than decoding out to the vocabulary. These latent ToM tokens are intended to summarize the partners likely reasoning given what the main agent can observe.

sections.title: 2.3 Self-Supervised Training via Self-Play
sections.content: TOM2VEC operates by teaching agents to predict latent vectors of each others thought traces. To obtain signal for this, we leverage self-play: given main agent (to be trained) and partner agent (both parameterized by the same model B), we sample reasoning trace from the partner, compress it into latent tokens, and then supervise the main agent to autoregressively produce latent tokens that match the latent tokens extracted from the partner. More formally, as illustrated in Figure 2 (Middle), given partner agents context cP , the partner Bθ(cP generates full reasoning sequence rP ). We first segment rP at sentence delimiters and store the hidden state of each token. To obtain continuous reasoning tokens, we reserve two positions for the start and end tokens and divide the sentences evenly into 2 chunks. We take the hidden state for the token at the center of each chunk to get 2 continuous latent tokens. We then add the hidden states from the tokens at the start and end of the reasoning trace, resulting in latent tokens. These tokens zt = (zt,start, zt,chunk 1, . . . , zt,chunk K-2, zt,end) = (zt,1, zt,2, . . . , zt,K) will serve as the targets for training the main agent. 3 Figure 2: Overview of TOM2VEC on the multi-party negotiation task. Left (training): From its local observation and interaction history, the main agent predicts continuous latent ToM tokens that summarize partners likely reasoning trace. Middle (training): The partners reasoning is segmented at sentence delimiters, and latent tokens are extracted across the trace. These vectors provide self-supervised targets for position-wise cosine alignment with the main agents predictions. Right (inference): The main agent predicts the latent ToM tokens using only its local context and conditions its subsequent reasoning and action on them. The partners private context and reasoning are used only to construct training targets. During training, all agents share model, so we can directly align the main agents output to the targets extracted from the partner. sections.title: 3.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Environments. We evaluate TOM2VEC on five multi-agent environments that span cooperative (Overcooked-AI, Hanabi, Collab Escape/Capture), mixed-motive (negotiation), and competitive (Decrypto) multi-agent settings. Overcooked-AI (Carroll et al., 2019) is fully cooperative cooking game in which two agents share kitchen and must interleave complementary subtasks (e.g., fetching onions, plating, and delivering) to maximize the total team score. We use three layouts provided in Carroll et al. (2019) (Cramped Room, Asymmetric Advantages, and Coordination Ring) each run for 30 seeds. Multi-party, multi-issue negotiation (Abdelnabi et al., 2024) is mixed-motive task that we evaluate over 100 samples where each agent holds private preferences over set of issues and must reach an agreement that balances their own selfinterest against the broader risk of walking away with no deal. Decrypto (Lupu et al., 2025) is competitive ToM communication game, in which decoder must interpret teammates clues relating to provided hint words (which only the decoder and teammate can view) while an interceptor simultaneously tries to recover the same hidden code from those clues; we run Decrypto over 1000 samples. We evaluate multiple environments from the LLM Coordination benchmark (Agashe et al., 2025). Hanabi is cooperative card game in which players can observe their teammates cards but not their own, requiring them to interpret limited hints to coordinate their actions; we run Hanabi over 100 seeds. In Collab Capture, two agents coordinate their movement and actions to capture an adversary. In Collab Escape, two agents must repair generators to open an exit while evading an adversary. In all environments, each agent receives only the observation permitted by its role, and cannot see their partners private contexts. Following Agashe et al. (2025), we evaluate Collab Capture and Collab Escape on 6 and 12 seeds respectively. Models. We use Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025), trained with TOM2VEC entirely in self-play with the partner instantiated from the same base model. To test the partner generality of the learned ToM, we additionally evaluate against partner agents drawn from other model families at test time, including Gemma-4-E4B (Google, 2026) and GPT5.4 (Singh et al., 2025), which are not seen during training, and the latter of which is far stronger.

sections.title: 3.2 Metrics
sections.content: We report each domains standard metrics. For Overcooked, we report mean episode score. For LLM Negotiation, we report deal-success rate (deal is acceptable for at least 5/6 parties) together with the agents own score and the average collective score across all parties. For Decrypto, we report the decoder win rate (how often the team guesses the codes), and interceptor win rate (how often the interceptor guesses the codes). For Hanabi, we report game score, which is the number of correctly played cards. For Collab Capture and Collab Escape, we report capture and escape success rates, respectively, together with average turn counts, following Agashe et al. (2025). strong ToM agent should improve across these tasks, which each require some form of partner modeling.

sections.title: 4 Discussion and Analysis
sections.content: The gains are partner-agnostic and transfer across model families. Although TOM2VEC is trained purely in self-play against Qwen3-8B partner, the observed gains on Overcooked persist when TOM2VEC is paired with unseen test-time partners  (Table 6)  . With strong GPT-5.4 partner, TOM2VEC improves over the base agent by 17.3 points on average, with positive gains on every layout. With Gemma-4 partner the improvement is smaller but still persists. This indicates that TOM2VEC learns generalized model of partner reasoning rather than overfitting to its training-time partner. This also highlights the generalizability of TOM2VEC to frontier model settings: we can train an agent against open-weight models and deploy it in teams with frontier models. TOM2VEC infers partner beliefs, desires, and actions more accurately. Beliefs: what the partner believes the agent is trying to do (a second-order inference). Desires: which subtask the partner is currently pursuing. Actions: which primitive action the partner will take next. code the components of theory-of-mind: it could be that some improved performance comes from learning to predict information correlated with partner actions, without formulating proper theory of the partner. Thus, following the Bayesian Theory of Mind decomposition of an agent into beliefs, desires, and actions (Baker et al., 2011), we directly check each agents model of its partner with three questions at sampled Overcooked states  (Table 7)  . Belief questions ask the agent what it thinks its partner thinks the agent (i.e., itself) is trying to do. Desire questions ask the partner what it currently wants to do. Action questions ask which action the partner will take next. Beliefs, desires, and actions each have six different options (based on the possible actions/steps within the Overcooked environment) to choose from, making this multiplechoice QA task, and test 300 samples per questions (see Appendix for prompts). We obtain ground truth labels by 1) continuing the partners generation and prompting it for its beliefs and desires and 2) directly taking the partners next action from its output. TOM2VEC achieves the highest accuracy on all three questions  (Table 7)  , improving over the next-best baseline by 5.6, 2.0, and 2.7 points. We test on the normal thoughts, altered layout (swapped real layout for alternate layout), and adversarial intent (partner agent is attempting to sabotage). tion type for every method as it is second-order ToM understanding capability (i.e., the agent must infer its partners theory about it). Latent ToM tokens encode valid partner-specific reasoning. We compare the perplexity the model assigns to the partners true reasoning when the ToM latents are derived from the partners actual context against two deliberately corrupted contexts: Altered Layout, in which the current layout is replaced with game state from another layout, and Adversarial Intent, in which the partner aims to hinder progress. The key assumption is that if the latents are capturing the partners reasoning, the generated thoughts from the true context should yield the lowest perplexity. We find that the Normal latents reach perplexity of 1.412, whereas both distractors are higher, at 1.702 and 1.613 for Altered Layout and Adversarial Intent respectively (see Table 8). Furthermore, the lowest perplexity is assigned to the correct CoT in 98.6% of cases with the true partner reasoning. Corrupting the partners context degrades how well the latents predict its reasoning, indicating that the latents are sensitive to valid partner-specific information.

sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Theory of Mind for LLM Agents. Theory of Mind is the capacity to infer the mental states of others, and is cornerstone of human social cognition (Premack and Woodruff, 1978). long line of work explores ToM in non-LLM agents (Gmytrasiewicz and Doshi, 2005; Pynadath and Marsella, 2005; Han and Gmytrasiewicz, 2018; Sequeira et al., 2025; He et al., 2025), which we do not discuss in detail, as our scope is LLM agents. In that context, large body of work tested the ToM capabilities of varying models (Le et al., 2019; Sap et al., 2022; Ullman, 2023; Kosinski, 2024; Xu et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2023), showcasing where LLMs succeed and fail in different aspects of ToM. Many past efforts have aimed to improve LLM ToM through inference-time prompting and decomposition, including perspective-taking prompts (Moghaddam and Honey, 2023; Wilf et al., 2024) and structured decomposition of the inference into sub-problems (Jung et al., 2024; Hou et al., 2024; Sarangi et al., 2025). related line of work augments models with explicit symbolic belief-tracking structures (Sclar et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025a; Tang and Belle, 2024). Outside of inference-time approaches, other previous approaches train LLMs to improve ToM (Sclar et al., 2025; Hwang et al., 2025). In contrast to these efforts, TOM2VEC learns latent partner representation supervised directly during self-play to facilitate broader understanding of the partner. Latent Reasoning Tokens. growing body of work has explored latent reasoning. paradigmatic example of this is Coconut (Hao et al., 2025), which feeds the models last hidden state back as the next input embedding, allowing single step to support several alternative continuations. Subsequent methods have enabled latent thinking by adjusting how latent thoughts are trained (Shen et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Su et al., 2025). Other attempts keep the model frozen and generate soft tokens that are projected into the LLMs representation space (Xu et al., 2025b,c) or use probabilityweighted embeddings (Zhang et al., 2026). Additionally, Gozeten et al. (2025) show how continuous CoTs enable parallel exploration better than discrete CoTs. Our work builds on prior work training latent reasoning models, especially findings that latent reasoning tokens can encode multiple paths. TOM2VEC is, to our knowledge, the first to explore this paradigm for modeling other agents, which poses distinct challenges (e.g., partial observability of other agents).

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced TOM2VEC, ToM method that trains an agent via self-play to model its partner via continuous thought tokens. Across five settings, both cooperative and competitive, TOM2VEC improves over all baselines and generalizes to partners not seen during training. Analysis indicates that TOM2VEC is able to make more accurate inferences about the partners state, indicating stronger ToM understanding. Taken together, the results suggest that modeling another agent in latent space is useful alternative to doing so in text.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: TOM2VEC requires access to the partners CoT during training. However, we show that this CoT does not need to come from the eventual test-time partner: training against one partner transfers to others. Nevertheless, it is still requirement of the training procedure, and our supervision relies on both agents sharing representation space, which is why training uses the same base model for agent and partner. TOM2VEC also requires training phase, unlike prompting-based approaches that work at inference time. We find this cost is offset by performance, since the method outperforms both prompting and training-matched verbalized baseline. Finally, we note that our experiments use English-only tasks, limitation shared with much prior work on LLM theory of mind and constrained in part by available models and datasets.

For Qwen3-8B, we set temperature of 1.0, top_p to 0.95, top_k to 20, repetition_penalty to 1.0, and presence_penalty to 1.5. sections.title: C Additional Results
sections.content: TOM2VEC obtains the strongest performance on ToM belief probing. more classic test of ToM is through reasoning on false agent beliefs. More concretely, whether an agent can recognize that another agent holds belief that differs from the true environment state. We evaluate this with Sally-Anne style belief test (Baron-Cohen et al., 1985). To test this, we create new Overcooked layout with custom cupboard tiles to test an agents ToM capabilities.

sections.title: A cupboard can be
sections.content: interacted with to store/retrieve an item, and the contents of cupboard are not visible at all times (i.e., the content must be retrieved to reveal the stored item). We place eight cupboards along the edge of the layout and fill the remaining edge tiles with walls. To conduct this test, we have an overseer agent observe two players within the environment act following set pattern. Player One takes three unique ingredients and stores each in three different cupboards. Player One exits and can no longer observe the scene. Player Two is given the item locations and chooses three random cupboards to move the ingredients to. Player Two exits, and player one enters. Now, given the games state history, we ask the overseer agent where it thinks Player One will look for each ingredient. We also independently ask the overseer agent where it believes the ingredients are after seeing them rearranged by player two to measure state understanding. We conduct this test on 50 different seeds and find that TOM2VEC scores 0.88  (Table 9)  , 0.14 improvement over the untrained agent, tying SelfConsistency for the best result and outperforming all other baselines. We also note that state understanding stays relatively consistent among the different methods, differing by 0.08 at most. Since all the methods retain similar levels of state understanding, the gains in partner state understanding are due to enhanced ToM capabilities rather than better overall state understanding. TOM2VEC exhibits belief revision given evidence. As kind of theory, theory-of-mind should be subject to rational revision given evidence. In Section 1 we pointed to the latent nature of TOM2VEC as core benefit in this regard: latent tokens more naturally lend themselves to representing multiple states, as has been shown for continuous reasoning tokens (Hao et al., 2025). Here, we test the ability of the latent tokens learned by TOM2VEC training to update given observations. Specifically, we construct novel Overcooked layout, shown in Figure 3, in which the agent (top, blue hat) and its partner (bottom, green hat) both start exactly in the middle, equidistant from the onion dispenser (west) and the dish dispenser (east). We then sample partner CoTs corresponding to different partners, one instructed to go to the onions Figure 3: We design custom layout and collect five east/west CoTs where the partner (green hat) decides to go either east towards the dish dispenser or west towards the onion dispenser. We calculate the perplexity of each CoT, plotted below. high east perplexity indicates that CoT corresponding to the dish dispenser is unlikely; low east perplexity means dish CoT is likely, and vice versa for west and onions. and the other to the dishes; we sample 5 CoTs per category. Following our perplexity analysis in Table 8, we compute the perplexity of these CoTs under the current set of latent tokens produced by the agent. Crucially, we score these CoTs as we move the partner east (closer to the dishes) or west (closer to the onions). At each step, the agent observes the partners movement history, starting from the center. rational agent should update its theory about its partner based on its movement; while priori the agent does not know whether the partner intends to go east or west, series of movements east (towards the dishes) should raise the probability of dish CoTs (i.e., lower their perplexity) while lowering the onion probability, and vice versa. Figure 3 shows precisely this trend: as the partner moves closer to each dispenser, the corresponding perplexities shift as expected. Promisingly, this indicates that not only does TOM2VEC teach agents to form snapshots of their partners, but it also teaches them to better update their theories given evidence. sections.title: Overcooked System Prompt
sections.content: You are an agent playing the cooperative cooking game Overcooked. You control one player in kitchen. Your goal is to cook and deliver soups as fast as possible. Game rules: - You earn reward only by DELIVERING soups whose ingredient set exactly matches one of the currently active orders. Each delivery yields sparse reward (default 20, can vary per layout). - You will only be able to interact with dispensers, pots, counters, or serving areas once you are facing them. Movement actions turn you; INTERACT acts on the cell directly in front. - You can only hold ONE item at time. To pick something else up, first place what you're holding on counter (X), or use it (drop ingredient into pot, deliver soup at S, etc.). How to cook and serve soup (the full loop): 1. PICK UP an ingredient: face an onion dispenser (O) or tomato dispenser (T) with empty hands and INTERACT. You now hold one onion / one tomato. 2. PLACE INGREDIENT IN POT: face pot (P) and INTERACT. The ingredient drops into the pot. pot holds at most 3 ingredients ('P1' / 'P2' / 'P3' shown on the map). 3. START COOKING: once the pot has the ingredients you want (1, 2, or 3), face the pot and INTERACT with empty hands to begin cooking. The pot shows 'P1*' / 'P2*' / 'P3*' while cooking and counts down (default 20 ticks; the prompt tells you ticks remaining). 4. GRAB DISH: face dish dispenser (D) with empty hands and INTERACT to hold dish. 5. PLATE THE SOUP: face the cooking pot once it shows 'P!' (ready) while holding dish, then INTERACT. You now hold soup with that pot's ingredients. 6. DELIVER: face serving area (S) while holding the soup and INTERACT. The order is fulfilled and reward is paid. Recipes / orders: - Only onions and tomatoes can be used as ingredients. recipe is the multiset of ingredients in the pot when you start cooking it. Order matters NOT, but the set must match an active order exactly. Common recipes are 3 onions, 3 tomatoes, or mixes (e.g. 2 onion + 1 tomato). - The "Active orders" list in the game state shows every recipe currently worth delivering. Build the pot to match one of them before starting to cook. - Adding the wrong ingredient to pot cannot be undone; once cooking starts, the recipe is locked. Coordination: - Two agents share the kitchen. Avoid blocking your partner or duplicating their work (e.g. both carrying onions to the same pot that's already full). - Counters (X) can be used as handoff: drop an item on counter for your partner to pick up. Movement and facing: - movement action (NORTH/SOUTH/EAST/WEST) ALWAYS updates your facing to that direction. After the action, your <dir> arrow on the map will point that way. - If the tile in that direction is walkable (' . '), you also move one cell there. - If that tile is blocked (counter, dispenser, pot, serving area, or another player), you DO NOT move -- you only turn to face it. Use this to line up an INTERACT. - To INTERACT with an object, you must first be facing it (the cell directly in front of your arrow). If you are not yet facing it, issue the direction action first to turn, then INTERACT on the next turn. - STAY leaves both your position and your facing unchanged. You will receive 2D ASCII map of the kitchen state and your past action history each turn. Each cell is 3 characters wide. (cid:44) Column indices (x) are printed above and below the grid; row indices (y) flank each row on the left and right. Read any position as (x, y). Terrain cells (a single character centered with spaces): ' . ' = walkable floor ' ' = onion dispenser ' ' = dish dispenser ' ' = serving area ' ' = counter (can place items) ' ' = tomato dispenser ' ' = empty pot Items sitting on counters / floor: ' ' = onion ' ' = tomato ' ' = dish ' ' = soup Pots in use: 'P1 ' / 'P2 ' / 'P3 ' = pot with 1 / 2 / 3 ingredients (not yet cooking) 'P1*' / 'P2*' / 'P3*' = pot currently cooking with that many ingredients 'P! ' = pot with ready (cooked) soup Players occupy 3-char cell '<idx><dir><held>': <idx> = agent index (0 or 1) -- you will be told which one is you 15 Overcooked System Prompt (continued) <dir> = '^' (NORTH), 'v' (SOUTH), '>' (EAST), '<' (WEST) <held> = 'o' onion, 't' tomato, 'd' dish, 's' soup, '.' nothing Example: '1^o' = agent 1 standing on floor tile, facing NORTH, holding an onion. Available actions (respond with EXACTLY one): NORTH EAST STAY - face up; move up if unblocked - face right; move right if unblocked WEST - keep position and facing SOUTH - face down; move down if unblocked - face left; move left if unblocked INTERACT - interact with the cell you are facing Choose the single best action given the current game state. Output only the action name, nothing (cid:44) else. Bayesian ToM Probing Prompts. We probe beliefs, desires, and next actions using the prompts below.
